rationale: A non-Parkinson extra-virgin versus refined trial gives a 4.22-point adjusted constipation difference favoring extra-virgin olive oil. In Parkinson disease, the KIM crossover and Brazilian counseling trial offered olive oil as part of both full patterns or broader counseling. Their controlled bowel estimates were inconclusive. The counseling supplement confirms the three-month timing. A Lithuanian composite Mediterranean score was associated with lower constipation odds. No available Parkinson trial isolates extra-virgin intake, so the lean still rests on the grade-specific comparison outside Parkinson disease.

A small baseline Parkinson association and a separate non-Parkinson observational estimate favor lower anxiety, with selection and multiplicity limitations. A cold-pressed trial lacks a verified oil-specific benefit. The KIM dietary phases share olive advice and show mixed ordinal anxiety changes. A diabetes support program reports a favorable anxiety outcome with olive oil as an option. A second Parkinson dietary-pattern study reports lower anxiety odds with a composite score. Neither intervention yields a pressing-specific comparison, leaving only the earlier minimal favorable lean.

A diabetes self-management protocol offers walnut oil as one optional ingredient and plans a depression scale. Available results leave the depression estimate and grade-specific use unavailable. No reviewed comparison measures depressive symptom change after cold-pressed walnut oil in Parkinson disease.

A mixed diabetes intervention offers peanut oil as one optional ingredient and plans a geriatric depression outcome. The body and depression comparison remain inaccessible. Actual use and refined grade are unverified. No reviewed source estimates the refined peanut oil effect on Parkinson depressive symptoms.

A diabetes support intervention reports a favorable anxiety direction for the program. The protocol offers peanut oil among several optional oils, with no reported cold-pressed grade, actual use or oil-specific comparison. The direction of anxiety severity after cold-pressed peanut oil in Parkinson disease remains unresolved.

Comparators using oral unspecified or refined oil, topical extra-virgin oil and population dietary estimates give only indirect sleep evidence. Both Parkinson KIM diets encouraged ungraded olive oil. A possible insomnia event during the ketogenic phase concerns the overall diet and the published denominators cannot establish a rate. The evidence leaves extra-virgin olive oil and Parkinson insomnia severity unresolved.
